item.title: Would you pay $58.5m to live in this iconic New York building?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20e5r1pvvdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Would you pay $58.5m to live in this iconic New York building? - Published The Flatiron Building - with its unique triangular shape, narrow prow, ornamental columns and intricate decorative details - has been one of the most recognisable structures in New York City for more than a century. But for the last seven years, the Flatiron has been shrouded in scaffolding, its Beaux-Arts exterior hidden from throngs of tourists who came to view it. It has been undergoing a large-scale renovation, both internal and external, from an awkwardly laid-out office building into ultra-luxury apartments - with new units going for up to $58.5m (£43.9m). Only 21 residences currently on the public market or under contract in New York City are priced higher, with the top spot occupied by a $128m (£96.1m) condo off Central Park, according to data compiled by Manhattan Miami Real Estate. Now, with its transformation nearly complete, the Flatiron is ready for its next - and most extravagant - phase of life. For over 120 years, the building has been a testament to architectural ingenuity, and while that history is highlighted in its redevelopment, the building is also becoming a symbol of just how expensive the city's luxury apartments can get. A dramatic impact on the neighbourhood The Flatiron Building's renaissance harkens back to when it was originally built. Completed in 1902, the building was an architectural marvel with a pioneering steel-frame construction making it one of the city's first skyscrapers. Designed by architect Daniel Burnham to fit onto a wedge-shaped plot of land at the intersection of Broadway and Fifth Avenue, it was initially dubbed "Burnham's Folly" because locals feared that its height and thinness would cause it to blow over. For years, tourists flocked to a small triangular park out front to snap a selfie with the full structure behind them. But after the scaffolding went up and the pandemic hit, the park saw a slight drop in visitors, said James Mettham, president of Flatiron NoMad Partnership, a business improvement district that operates the park space. As the scaffolding has come down, he says the visitors have returned. "People are coming back to get their pictures, and then in turn will go shop at the local retail, and all the great food and beverage that's around here," Mettham said. "So getting it back in all of its glory to complement everything that's been going on around it is really important." Originally built to house the Fuller Company, a Chicago construction firm, the 24-storey, 94m (307ft) tall building has had many occupants, including clothing and toy companies, magazines, and publishing houses. But in its 100-plus-year history, it was always an office space – until now. After the last office tenants, Macmillan Publishing, moved out in 2019, scaffolding went up and it sat vacant through years of ownership disputes. The building's current owners – the Brodsky Organization, GFP Real Estate, and the Sorgente Group - began renovations in 2023, after announcing they would convert it into high-end condos. Once completed, the building will have 36 open-concept apartments – some half-floor and some full-floor units – ranging from $11m (£8.3m) for three-bedroom units to $58.5m (£43.9m) for a full-floor five-bedroom residence with a balcony, which is currently in contract. Amenities also are being added to the building's basement and common spaces, including a 18m (60 ft) pool, billiards room and piano lounge, and wellness centre. New residents are expected to start moving in in the coming months, the owners say. All units and amenities are expected to be finished in early 2027. How do you make a triangular residence desirable? When New York design firm Studio Sofield was hired to reimagine the building's interior, it had to address the problem of the building's previous life as an office space, co-founder William Sofield said. Another big hurdle came with the building's shape. How do you subdivide a triangle – just 1.8m (6ft) across at its narrowest point - into luxury apartments worthy of a multimillion-dollar price tag? But the triangle itself – along with its history, architectural ingenuity, and novelty – is exactly the point. "It wasn't about changing anything that makes the building so special and beloved to New Yorkers," Thomas Brodsky, partner at the Brodsky Organization, told the BBC. "The layouts and the proportions and views really came directly from the architecture rather than from how we generally would start planning a building from the ground up." Originally designed to evoke a classic Greek column, the structure's limestone, brick and terra-cotta exterior features ornamentation including lion heads, wreaths, eagles, and faces. Beyer Blinder Belle, lead developer on the building's exterior, enlisted a speciality manufacturer in California to replicate and restore thousands of terra-cotta pieces from the facade, reinstalling each by hand. The building's windows, totalling over 1,000, also needed to be replaced – dating back to the 1970s, they were too heavy, hard to open, and not energy efficient. The new ones are thick enough to block the bustling noise of surrounding streets, offering silence in units that's uncharacteristic of New York City apartments. Steel beams holding up the skyscraper are exposed in various corners of residential units - an homage to what made the original building so innovative. In the 12th-floor model unit, the steel framework has even been turned into closet shelving. The scaffolding is expected to be fully removed by the end of summer. When the restored exterior is unveiled for the first time in seven years and illuminated for the first time ever, everyone will get to appreciate its beauty, said Mettham. "Whether it's functioning as an office for one of the world's largest publishing companies, or it happens to have really expensive condos," he said, sitting in a small park at the building's prow, "the exterior, and what we see from these spaces right here, we share in that. We are all part of that." Old menus, a hidden balcony and a wooden revolving door The redevelopment led to some unexpected discoveries. While removing sheetrock during demolition, workers found remnants of a balcony at the triangular point on the 20th floor, identical to an existing balcony one floor above. "It's kind of the hidden jewel in the building that nobody knew about," said Carlos Cardoso, partner at Beyer Blinder Belle. That balcony, overlooking the treetops of Madison Square Park and the length of Broadway, has now been restored. Going through the building's cavernous basement – which once housed two restaurants – crews found fragments of a wooden, revolving door dating back to the 1910s. That door was so damaged that it couldn't be salvaged, Cardoso said, so it was replicated. The building's developers have found other ways to incorporate the building's past into its new life. Steel balustrades from an old staircase found in the basement were repurposed as legs for apartments' bathroom sinks. Mosaic tile lettering on the floors marking each apartment number is a recreation of the originals. Other artifacts found in the basement – tools, a piano, original restaurant menus, shoes, advertisements, shirts, lights, and buckets – will be displayed in glass cases in the lobby, giving modern dwellers a glimpse of Flatiron's past. A "nearly forgotten" historic streetlamp that once stood outside on 23rd Street has been reimagined as a chandelier in the lobby, Sofield said. Paneling from one of the building's original restaurants was recreated in the trim of the new pool. Vintage planters and awnings as well as antique light fixtures and window curtains are being incorporated into the street fronts. And the building's entire facade – with its unique form and intricate detailing - will be showcased with new lights, allowing passersby to admire it at night. "Unlike many buildings in New York, the Flatiron is seen in the round," Sofield said. "All sides are extraordinary."

item.title: What Love Island tells us about the changing face of dating
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c935q2k6pxqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
On the fourth series of Love Island UK in 2018, Megan Barton-Hanson pulled fellow Islander, Wes Nelson, for a chat. Just moments earlier, she had ended her relationship with Eyal Booker after admitting the pair had little more than physical chemistry. Now, sitting opposite Wes, who had been coupled up with Laura Anderson since the start of the competition, she decided not to wait for him to make the first move. "I think it's pretty obvious that I do really fancy you," she told him. "And I just felt like, if I didn't say something, I'd regret it massively." By the end of the episode, viewers had a new nickname for her: "Muggy Megan". Critics accused her of moving too quickly between relationships and breaking "girl code". Others admired her honesty. At the time, Barton-Hanson argued that she had been treated differently to her male counterparts. "People definitely do give girls a harder time than men… It's sexist." But eight years later, scenes like Barton-Hanson's no longer feel quite so out of the ordinary. Until this series, the opening coupling had always seen the men choose first. This year, the shows rules were changed, with the women making the first choice. Alicia Denby, a sociologist at Manchester Metropolitan University, argues the show's tweak is reflective of a broader societal change where "women may now be more likely to approach someone first". At its peak, around five million people tuned in to Love Island every night. Live audiences are not what they were, but it remains ITV's biggest programme among 16 to 34-year-olds. For Prof Kitty Nichols, who researches relationships and popular culture at the University of Sheffield, Love Island has become "an important cultural vehicle" allowing us to "reflect on the dating scene and culture at the moment". Former PE teacher Kai Fagan met his now wife, Sanam Harrinanan, when he won the 2023 series, an experience he says transformed his life. "My life ever since then has been a fairytale. The whole show is about love. That's the point of it. You're put in a situation to fall in love." For Fagan, the show delivered exactly what it promised: love. Meanwhile, for thousands watching at home, it has become a window into how modern relationships are formed, tested and understood. As another series of Love Island approaches its end, what do Love Island's changing dynamics tell us about dating culture beyond the villa? And does women making the first move really represent genuine progress towards equality? The forever changing rules For much of the 20th Century, heterosexual dating followed a script that would have felt familiar to the characters in Pride and Prejudice. Men were largely expected to make the first move. They asked women out, paid for dates and, in many cases, took the lead in deciding when the relationship moved forward. By the 1960s, the women's liberation movement began challenging many of those norms. As Aretha Franklin's Respect became an anthem for a generation demanding greater equality, the widespread availability of contraception changed the ideas about sex. Then with the rise of online dating in the 2000s, millions of people began meeting through websites and, later, dating apps. But whether these changes have really done anything to shift gender expectations is unclear. As recently as 2021, sociologist Ellen Lamont reviewed more than 100 studies on heterosexual dating and found traditional dating scripts still remained, with men still expected to make the first move. For cultural commentator Coco, who goes by her first name and has amassed more than 100,000 followers on TikTok analysing Love Island, this reflects an important distinction. She argues women aren't replacing men as the pursuers, they simply have greater freedom to act on what they want. "Women haven't flipped the roles," she says. "Women have just been allowed to exist." She believes women now have "more choice, freedom and opportunity than we've ever had in history". Love Island's contradiction But even if women are becoming more comfortable making the first move, Denby argues that this does not mean gendered power relations have disappeared. She argues that women on Love Island are often praised for their patience and loyalty while male contestants explore connections with other contestants. But she says when women take a more active role in pursuing relationships, they are judged differently. "It's almost as if women are praised for being submissive in the villa, because when they do take on more of an active or expressive role, they are criticised for it." On this year's Love Island, in a move that may have reflected the growing trend of women on the show taking the lead, Elicia Bailey took both Aidan Murphy and Finley Maddock to the Hideaway, the villa's private romantic room. But she faced criticism for it and Denby points to what she sees as a sexual double standard around women's sexuality. Another female contestant on this year's show, Priya Jaswal, was labelled a "sexual person" by a male contestant and accused of "pouncing" on Murphy, comments that Denby argues, suggest "women are judged for taking an active role" in dating. Nichols sees similar patterns. She believes Love Island has what she describes as "pockets of diversity" and "little moments of change", where contestants challenge conventional gender roles. Yet she argues those moments are often temporary, with Islanders reverting "back to the expected gender roles". According to Nichols, double standards persist. "If a woman behaves in the same way that a man behaves, they get reprimanded." That reaction can be seen in the programme's history. For example, Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu's pursuit of Jay Younger divided viewers during the 2022 series. Some accused her of betraying Davide Sanclimenti, who she later won the show with, while others praised her confidence. For Nichols, those responses reveal something about British attitudes to dating. "I think audience members receive more positively men diverging from their expected roles," she says. She said it may be because viewers "don't anticipate" behavior like that, But adds that, "sometimes women doing so is sort of seen less positively." What happens when the rules change? For Tareq Ferguson, a long-time Love Island viewer and TikTok commentator with more than 50,000 followers, one of the biggest changes in recent series has been watching male contestants become more passive. "The men want to be passenger princesses," he says. "They want to sit back, kick up their feet, while the women do the grafting and do the work." On this year's show, Lorenzo Alessi was reluctant to make Julia Majchrzak a morning coffee, something many contestants see as an act of care for the person they're coupled up with. It become a flashpoint on the show and sparked debate among viewers. For Ferguson, moments like those reflect a wider shift in modern dating, with some men appearing increasingly hesitant to take the lead. But some research suggest that men's reluctance may stem less from disinterest and more from uncertainty about how to navigate dating today. In a recent Cosmopolitan survey, men said online dating had made then feel judged on their appearance. While others said repeated rejection and lack of matches had damaged their confidence. Research like this echoes what Coco believes is happening both inside and outside the villa. "Society has rightly expanded what's possible for women," she says. "But we haven't spent the same amount of time helping young men understand what their role looks like in this landscape. The cultural conversation hasn't kept pace with the social change." She also believes online conversations have contributed to that uncertainty. "I think the manosphere content we're seeing has done something to women," she says. "It's put their guard up." But she is keen to stress that does not mean there are "no good men out there". Instead, she believes men seem to be taking a more cautious approach to dating as expectations around relationships continue to change. "They don't want to be perceived as a creep. They don't want to be seen as trying too hard in front of their peers. They want to come across as relaxed and cool." What does Love Island tell us about modern dating? So does Love Island simply mirror the UK's evolving dating culture or actively shape it? For Prof Nichols, the two are closely connected. She believes the programme doesn't simply entertain audiences. Watched by millions each summer and discussed constantly across social media, it has become part of the conversation around modern relationships. "I think for young people who are still the biggest viewers of Love Island, it probably creates these norms for them in terms of how they would expect to be treated or how dating functions." Fagan believes some younger viewers take lessons from what they see on screen. "Younger people probably get dating tips from a show like Love Island," he says. But he adds: "In real life, you have a bit more control of how you pursue and what happens and the obstructions. "On Love Island, you could be with someone for three weeks and then suddenly you're put into a challenge where your relationship is made vulnerable just for the entertainment of the public. "If that's happening on the outside, you don't necessarily know about it. On the show, you have to confront it head on." Yet despite those differences, some viewers still believe Love Island influences how people think about dating. Ferguson believes many young people watch the programme not just as entertainment but as a reflection of what dating now looks like. "People will look at this, especially the younger audiences, and think, 'if this is how people are being treated, then obviously I can expect this on the outside.'" One study by researchers at Liverpool John Moores University examining Love Island and relationship education, found some young people do look to reality dating programmes for ideas about romance and relationship behaviour. But it also found most viewers described the programme as entertainment and were aware that what they watched did not necessarily reflect real life. For Nichols, the influence is undeniable. "It plays into features of the current dating culture, where we see this propensity towards disposability and a lack of exclusivity," she says. "It's like a chicken and an egg. I think it normalises that massively." More than a dating show Every generation has tended to challenge the dating expectations that came before it. From the move away from formal courtship to the arrival of dating apps and now a generation asking more questions about who should make the first move. But while analysts argue that Love Island is far from a perfect mirror of society, it nonetheless operates as a cultural stage where shifting gender norms and emerging challenges are publicly rehearsed. For Denby, that is precisely what makes the show significant. "Recouplings, comparisons between potential partners and the idea that there is always someone better around the corner can mirror some of the less positive aspects of app-based dating culture", she says. But she is equally clear that viewers are not watching the programme without question. "I don't think viewers are simply passive consumers. Many people watch Love Island critically and debate issues like sexism, classism and racism, so the programme both reflects and shapes contemporary dating culture." item.title: Pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein - how Italian children became so overweight
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c33y3151vydo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein - how Italian children became so overweight - Published Daily life is not easy for Salvatore. At 17, he weighs 170kg (26st 10lb) and struggles to walk. He can't tie his own shoelaces and his Vespa scooter strains to bear his weight - in one week, its wheels broke seven times. "He eats constantly," says his mother Anna. Salvatore is among a growing number of Italian children and teenagers living with obesity. The problem is particularly acute in the south: in parts of the Campania region, more than 40% of eight and nine-year-olds are overweight. The town of Ponticelli, on the outskirts of Naples, has earned the unenviable reputation as one of the world's child obesity capitals. It is a striking development in a country long regarded as the spiritual home of the Mediterranean diet. Yet today, Italian children are among the most overweight in Europe, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Salvatore is waiting for life-changing surgery at the Betania Hospital in Ponticelli, where Dr Sonja Chiappetta has spent 15 years treating patients with severe obesity. Until recently, she says, most of her patients were in their fifties. "Now I see those same patients when they're teenagers, as young as 16. They are getting younger, and it's frightening." The surgery she carries out removes up to 90% of the stomach - meaning people are unable to eat large quantities of food. Demand has risen sharply in this part of Italy. But Salvatore has been told he cannot get the operation. His weight is so excessive it makes the surgery too dangerous. Instead, Dr Chiappetta has prescribed him a GLP-1 weight-loss injection to reduce his appetite and help him lose enough weight for the operation. For decades, Italy was held up as a model of healthy eating. The Mediterranean diet - rich in vegetables, legumes, olive oil, whole grains and fish - became famous after US physiologist Ancel Keys and his wife, biochemist Margaret Keys, studied communities in southern Italy in the 1950s and linked their habits to remarkably low rates of heart disease. Their research transformed a regional way of eating into one of the world's best-known diets; a blueprint for healthy living. But the Italy that inspired those studies no longer exists. "The traditional Mediterranean diet has been lost," says Doctor Valter Longo, director of the Longevity Institute at the University of Southern California. "Only 10% of Italians really follow it." Dr Longo sums up the modern Italian diet with what he calls the "five Ps": pizza, pasta, potatoes, protein and pane - the Italian word for bread. The transformation is visible everywhere: from supermarket shelves stocked with ultra-processed foods to pizzerias selling slices piled high with chips, sausages and fried snacks. Doctor Roberto Berni Canani, a paediatrician and obesity specialist at the Federico II University in Naples, sees the consequences every day. "I've treated children who are just two or three years old and already weigh 25kg," he says. He says most parents don't recognise their children are overweight. "They come to see me because of other problems - a cough, stomach pain, diarrhoea. They don't realise their child's weight is what's causing it." Italy’s child obesity time-bomb Italian children have become some of the most overweight in Europe, despite the country being famous for the so-called Mediterranean diet. What can be done to help them? Ten-year-old Francesca has a persistent cough and struggles to swallow. Doctors suspect an inflammatory condition of the oesophagus. She weighs 60kg (9st 6lb) - but that's not why her parents have sought medical help. Francesca says she eats bread with Nutella for breakfast, a chocolate-filled sponge cake as a snack, pasta with lentils for lunch and usually chicken for dinner. "But she doesn't eat vegetables," her mother, Carmen, interjects. "I put them in front of her, but she won't touch them." Francesca's parents insist she is active. She does artistic gymnastics and Latin dance, and doesn't get tired. They have never considered her weight as a problem. Dr Berni Canani reaches a different conclusion. The problem, he explains, is the overall pattern rather than any single meal. Small, calorie-dense foods consumed throughout the day, sugary drinks, too few fruit and vegetables and little understanding of how these habits accumulate over time. "This is a very good mother," he says. "A very good father. They simply don't recognise the importance of diet quality and body weight." By the time many families arrive at his clinic, unhealthy habits have already become deeply ingrained. They begin at home and are reinforced at school. And in Italy, encouraging children to be more active can be surprisingly difficult. Many schools are housed in beautiful old palazzi - they were never designed with modern physical education in mind. The Ugo Foscolo primary school is no exception. Its gym has barely enough space for a class of children to move around. "I have one pupil I'm particularly concerned about," says Francesca Pecce, who teaches at the school. "He's 10 years old and weighs around 60 kilograms." She has tried raising the issue with his mother. "But she is not worried," Pecce says. "In Neapolitan culture, if a child is a little chubby with rosy cheeks, people often think they're healthy." Schools, she believes, can help change that, especially if children "take home" lessons about healthy eating. "Sometimes it's easier to educate the parents through their children than the other way round." At a secondary school in Naples, students file into a classroom for a nutrition workshop run by the Valter Longo Foundation. The programme is part of a regional initiative to tackle childhood obesity. Over the coming months, more than 17,000 students across 25 schools will take part. Families will receive support to help change eating habits at home. But not all of the students are convinced. Eighteen-year-old Ciro doubts that information alone will change behaviour. "My classmates already know what's healthy," he says. "They just don't care." Carmen, 19, is more optimistic. "I thought it was actually really helpful because teenagers today are really big into junk food, and don't exercise as much." She says the problem is that temptation is everywhere. Even foods traditionally associated with Italy have changed. "When we go out for pizza, people don't just order a Margherita. They put chips, sausages and fried food on top." Add to that the centuries-old cliches of Italian mothers and grandmothers showing their love through food, and it's a perfect storm. Obesity is an "escalating global epidemic", says the WHO. More than one billion people worldwide are now obese, and childhood obesity has quadrupled since 1990. In 2025, Italy became the first country to pass a national law recognising obesity as a chronic, progressive and relapsing disease. Rather than treating obesity simply as the result of poor choices, the country's new law recognises it as a chronic disease influenced by biology, environment and social circumstances. The Campania region has become a testing ground for putting that philosophy into practice, implementing a series of ambitious interventions - including a controversial trial of a "fast-mimicking diet". Researchers are recruiting 300 overweight adolescents who will spend five days every three months on a controlled diet of 1,100 calories on day one and 770 calories on following four days - so restrictive it resembles a fast. The goal is to trigger a "metabolic reset". "Fasting, or controlled deprivation of food, is linked to a longer and healthier lifespan," says Dr Longo, who has spent three decades studying the effects of fasting. But not all obesity specialists are persuaded that fasting is the right approach for children. Paediatrician Berni Canani believes the evidence for fasting-mimicking diets in children is still too limited to be recommended in Italy's clinical guidelines. He also worries restrictive diets could carry psychological risks for adolescents, whose relationship with food is still developing. "I fear that imposing food restrictions on teenagers could increase the risk of eating disorders, anorexia and body dysmorphia," he says. Meanwhile, Salvatore hopes to have surgery in the summer, so that, for the first time in years, he can wear a swimming costume without feeling self-conscious. But he is not alone. Across Italy, a generation of children is growing up increasingly removed from the Mediterranean diet that once made the country famous. Additional reporting by Bob Howard. ========================================
Smash hit: How Alex Eala's Wimbledon run made everyday Filipinos fall in love with tennis - Published Chasing her dream of becoming a world tennis champion, teen athlete Maristella Torrecampo and her father took a gruelling 13-hour bus from her sleepy hillside hometown for her latest match in Manila. The 14-year-old's mum and four siblings could not join to watch her play; her crowdfunded budget was only enough for two round-trip bus tickets and a few days' worth of meals. Barely rested from the long journey, and with only her father cheering her on, Torrecampo crushed her Omani opponent in straight sets 6-1, 6-1 on that sweltering Tuesday afternoon at the Rizal Stadium, keeping alive her dream of following in the footsteps of Alexandra Eala, the country's newest sports star. Torrecampo competed in Manila in July as the Philippines was celebrating Eala's historic Wimbledon run - one that Torrecampo and the entire nation followed on streaming and social media. Eala, 21, went the farthest any Filipina had gone in a Grand Slam event, reaching the fourth round and eliminating defending champion Iga Swiatek of Poland along the way. Since her breakout semi-final performance at the Miami Open last year, Eala has re-ignited interest in tennis in the Philippines, a country obsessed with the three B's - basketball, boxing and beauty queens. To young tennis players like Torrecampo, Eala is an inspiration. "Like Ate Alex, I want to win at Wimbledon, WTA, and various tournaments around the world," Torrecampo said, referring to Eala with the Filipino word for elder sister. "She inspired me so much. I looked up to her since I was little," said Torrecampo, who has competed in the Philippine National Games, and in tournaments in Cambodia and Sri Lanka. "I like her attitude off and on court. Off court, she is really humble. There are a lot of kids like me who look up to her." Eala came home from London to a hero's welcome, with President Ferdinand Marcos hosting a reception in her honour at Malacanang Palace in Manila. "I'm so grateful that I am able to share my triumphs, most especially my recent run at Wimbledon, with the country," Eala said at the reception. "As we say, this is our victory. I cannot begin to describe how overjoyed I am to see how my progress has been received by the Filipino people." Such recognition from her compatriots, Eala added, made her feel "very seen". A rich man's sport Tennis is an elite sport in the Philippines, an archipelago nation of 112 million people. Decades of American colonial rule bequeathed the nation with a passion for basketball. Every village has a basketball court and Filipinos are more likely to recognise LeBron James than Roger Federer. Filipinos' love for rags-to-riches underdog stories and big personalities have also made boxing and beauty pageants just as popular. Boxing legend Manny Pacquiao is still the country's most popular athlete. Tennis has historically been much less popular - until Eala burst onto the scene. But this has also exposed how difficult it is for everyday Filipinos to take up the sport. Tennis courts are usually found in rich enclaves and equipment is expensive. Court rentals in Manila cost around 2,000 pesos ($32; £19) per hour, meaning half a day's play costs half the minimum wage. Even for higher income earners, that's equivalent to a month's worth of groceries. Tennis coach Jovy Barce knows how hard it is to start playing tennis from scratch, especially for the underprivileged. Barce told the BBC he started as a ball boy picking up balls on the court as a six-year-old in Caloocan city, on the capital's outskirts. He said players would pay him 100 pesos or roughly two dollars, which he would split between himself and his mum for their household's groceries. Then, when he was eight, Barce picked up a tennis racket from the bin and started practising. Later, one of the players on the court gave him his old racket. "Up until this day, I couldn't explain how happy I was when I got it. I used it over and over until I became so confident," Barce said. "No one taught me. I never had a professional coach. It was all self-study." Barce put himself through college on a sports scholarship. He worked at a hotel and as a motorcycle delivery man, but eventually pursued a career in tennis coaching, starting with just 40 tennis balls. "I started from nothing, but I tried my best to learn everything because I really wanted to become a coach," he said. "I practised every day. I was always focused. I did not have the chance to compete abroad since I do not have the money or big sponsors. I only competed in Metro Manila and provinces nearby." Eala, meanwhile, has been criticised for her elite background. She studied tennis at the Rafael Nadal Academy in Spain. Her mother is a former telecommunications executive while her father is a businessman from a prominent family. Eala was also seen dancing onstage with Bad Bunny during the Puerto Rican star's concert in Sweden. But she has taken such criticisms in stride, saying critics fail to see her hard work behind the scenes. Tennis rises in the Philippines Eala's homecoming from Wimbledon showed how big a star she has become. Big name sponsors mounted fan events, including a meet-and-greet at a shopping mall in Metro Manila's business district of Makati. Many came with their families. Some, like Federico Perez and his wife Gilia, drove hours from nearby provinces. The couple booked a hotel to get to the event early and secure the best possible view, even though they didn't have tickets. "We hope to see Alex in person and hopefully she can sign this. Even if this magazine was published a year ago, I still bought it because it has Alex on the cover," Gilia Perez said. She said her husband never fails to watch Eala's Wimbledon matches, even if they air in the Philippines late at night. Eleven-year-old Luca Ong, a young tennis fan, came with his parents. "My goal in the future is to become the next Alex Eala or Rafa Nadal so that I can represent the Philippines in the future," he said. Eala's hot streak has also energised tennis hobbyists. At a Manila tennis court, Celso Mugot said his determination to learn the sport had intensified because of Eala's success. The 33-year-old accountant has been training for three months to keep fit and unwind after work. "I was definitely inspired by Alex Eala. I saw her progress. I watched her when she was still in a low rank until she climbs up," Mugot told the BBC. Rafael Santos, a 29-year-old information technology professional, also recently took up tennis as a sport. He said booking tennis courts had been difficult since Eala's breakout Miami Open run last year. "There are only a few courts in Manila while there are a lot of people who wanted to play and train. That's a bit of a let-down," Santos said. He said tennis shoes and apparel were also either sold out or in short supply, and some stores had jacked up racket prices. Felino Palafox, a renowned Filipino architect and urban planner, told the BBC that space was a major challenge in building more tennis courts. Metro Manila is home to close to 16 million people and is one of the world's most densely populated urban centres. Meanwhile, every village in the Philippines has a basketball court that is easily converted into a beauty pageant runway, and boxing gyms run by prizefighters are spread across major cities. "Ideally, every barangay (village) should have a tennis court, not just basketball courts," Palafox told the BBC. "We are fighting for (space for) activities." Just getting started Eala is now preparing for the US Open in August, seeking to raise the Philippines' status in tennis even higher. "That's a wrap on Manila. Thank you for welcoming me, my countrymen," she said in an Instagram story. "Each and every one of your stories has touched me on a profound level. I leave with a refreshed memory of what I carry when I'm out there playing tennis. And wow, is it a privilege to be part of something bigger than myself. Never been prouder to represent home." The journey continues too for Torrecampo, the 14-year-old from Iriga city. She said she would be working on calming her pre-match nerves as much as improving her swing. "I hope that aspiring tennis players would get to reach their dreams too, to become professional tennis players, because more kids will get inspired when they see people achieve great things in tennis," she said. Her father and coach, Delfin Torrecampo, said he would let her daughter enjoy the sport to ease the pressure she usually feels. "What I always tell her is to focus on the game. Do whatever you can do, but do not pressure yourself. Even if you know you can beat your opponent, do not be complacent," he told the BBC. "To people who are in the same situation as us, know that poverty is not a hindrance for you and your family's dreams. The people who keep on fighting and persevering are the same people who have the chance to win. "You may not win today or tomorrow, but your win will come one day as long as you keep on fighting."

item.title: CJP protest: The youth movement India's Modi didn't see coming
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07rgpxe51no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
CJP protest: The youth movement India's Modi didn't see coming - Published It began with a fear familiar to millions of young Indians: if the examinations that determine their future cannot be trusted, what can? Weeks later, on Monday, tens of thousands of young men and women tried to march on India's parliament. Police responded with tear gas and baton charges. Thousands more have returned to the streets in the days since. The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-led movement born out of anger over repeated examination paper leaks, quickly became India's biggest student mobilisation in years. It demanded education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Hours after Pradhan resigned on Saturday following weeks of protests over exam paper leaks and testing irregularities, the CJP called off its agitation, saying the government had accepted its demands. At its centre was activist Sonam Wangchuk, who lost 11kg (24lb) during a 26-day hunger strike in support of the movement before ending his fast on Thursday. The obvious question is whether this is simply another student protest - or the beginning of something larger. History offers reasons for both caution and optimism. Student movements have periodically transformed Indian politics. The Nav Nirman agitation in Gujarat helped trigger veteran socialist leader Jayaprakash Narayan's movement against former prime minister Indira Gandhi in the 1970s. Others have erupted dramatically before fading away. What makes the CJP unusual, however, is not simply its scale but the nature and breadth of its grievance. Unlike many of the biggest protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government over the past decade - whether over citizenship, farm laws or other contentious policies - this movement is not fundamentally about ideology. Nor is it rooted in the interests of a single community or social group. Instead, it questions whether the state can still guarantee fairness in the examination system that millions of young Indians see as their principal route to social mobility. "The exam and education system cuts across caste, class and gender to quite a large degree," Yamini Aiyar, Senior Visiting Fellow at Brown University, told the BBC. "The core constituency coming to these protests doesn't represent a singular interest group." That breadth is also what makes the movement politically distinctive. - Why are thousands protesting for education reform in India? - Published2 days ago
- The hunger-striking engineer demanding education reforms in India - Published5 days ago
"This movement centres on administrative failure," Rahul Verma, a fellow at the Centre for Policy Research, a Delhi-based think tank, told the BBC. "The state's inability to conduct examinations fairly and prevent paper leaks makes it a very different kind of political challenge to the BJP." That difference, he argues, changes the politics. Unlike earlier protests rooted in ideology or policy, this one questions the BJP's ability to govern. "They must recalibrate their strategy," Verma says. Many of those protesting, he adds, are not natural opponents of the BJP. They are "aspirational young Indians and their parents who see these exams as a path to upward mobility". Because the grievance is about governance rather than ideology, he argues, the BJP cannot easily rally its supporters or deploy the political counter-narratives that helped it confront earlier protest movements. Monday's demonstrations appeared to reinforce that assessment. For the past two weeks, comparisons with the anti-corruption movement of 2011 had largely centred on the CJP's impressive online reach, while sceptics questioned whether digital momentum could spill onto the streets. Monday's turnout suggested it could. Joyojeet Pal, a professor at the University of Michigan who studies technology and society, says social media has become "a tinderbox waiting to explode with the next thing", its speed and reach driven by emotion. Long-simmering frustration over the state's lack of accountability created the conditions for this "implosion", he told the BBC, adding that the architecture of social media makes such eruptions likely to recur. - How exam scandals threaten the future of India's young people - Published24 June 2024
The question now is whether that online surge has become something more enduring. "I think Monday's gathering indicates this movement may have crossed a tipping point," Verma says. Whether it grows from here, he adds, will depend largely on how the government responds. For Aiyar, Monday's protests revealed something equally significant. Student unions, Left groups and organisations such as the Bhim Army, a Dalit rights group, were present, but they were ultimately "outnumbered by an organic outpouring of students from all over the country". "That's unique compared to any significant protest in India's recent history," she says. Just as significantly, Aiyar believes the movement has already outgrown the organisation that sparked it and Wangchuk's hunger strike. "The catalyst may have been the CJP," she says, "but it became bigger than them." Students came not only because of the state's handling of the protests, she argues, but because they wanted "a space and a site to express the deep frustration" they had been carrying for some time. "The memes, posters and slogans suggested grievances extending well beyond exam paper leaks." After initially leaving the response to ministers and party spokespersons, the ruling BJP party's top leadership stepped in on Wednesday. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh accused the opposition of using students "as a political tool" while insisting the government remained committed to addressing their concerns through parliament. Modi addressed the issue publicly for the first time on Thursday. "Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth," he wrote on X, announcing fast-track courts to ensure "swift and stringent punishment" for those involved in paper leaks. "Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared." Whether those assurances will be enough to defuse the protests remains uncertain. Aiyar believes the movement has tapped into broader anxieties over a slowing economy, scarce jobs and a deepening sense that the future offers diminishing opportunities. "There is deep economic dissatisfaction and distress, which has translated into a lack of hope about the future," Aiyar says. "This could reflect growing exhaustion with a government that has been in power for a long time. Its failure to deliver on the promises it built its reputation on may have reached a tipping point." For her, the protests are about far more than a single policy failure. "The message from protesters is clear: we're exhausted. We need a new kind of politics, a new political grammar - one rooted in ideas and focused on governance and delivery." Whether that frustration can be sustained as a political movement, however, is another question. Political scientist Suhas Palshikar argues the Cockroach movement may simply provide an outlet for public anger before gradually losing steam, much like the farmers' protests. "Where will the Cockroach movement go? Perhaps nowhere - it will allow venting of frustration and taper off," he wrote on X. He also cautions against romanticising it as a Gen Z uprising. "It would be a mistake to imagine a youth movement or a Gen Z movement - these are only convenient myths for commentators." The movement's "ideological and political character... is currently fluid", he argues, with different political forces likely to seek influence over it. What the protesters have undeniably shown, he says, is a willingness to confront the state. "The young have shown their angst and their disgust. They have borne the brunt of the democratic government's brutal police. They have also shown that only street action makes this regime... listen and talk." Whether that energy can endure, Palshikar argues, will depend on many factors, including state repression, media blackouts, leadership challenges and the difficulty of building a broad social coalition. Economist Surajit Mazumdar of Delhi's Jawaharlal Nehru University also believes the movement already points to something much larger than examination paper leaks. "The current protest and the spontaneous response it has evoked is indicative of the widespread discontent of young people and students about the state of affairs in the country and in the education system which goes beyond the specific paper leak issue," he told the BBC. Compared with earlier student mobilisations, he argues, the current movement appears "broader and larger in scale". Mazumdar also rejects the idea that the protests are post-ideological. Like the farmers' movement before them, he says they show that "the democratic spirit is still alive in Indian society". For Aiyar, that democratic impulse is already reshaping politics. "People are seeking accountability for governance in sites that are non-electoral," Aiyar says. "The split between electoral legitimacy and democratic accountability outside electoral space is the new phenomenon of politics in India." The Cockroach Janta Party has called off its protests after securing the education minister's resignation. Whether that becomes a turning point for democratic accountability in India - or simply a rare political concession - will become clear only with time.

Families still search for bodies a month after Venezuela earthquakes Families in Venezuela are still searching for the remains of their loved ones, lost amid the rubble of flattened apartment buildings that line the coast of La Guaira, the region worst-hit by twin earthquakes on 24 June. Government officials say the death toll has surpassed 5,300, though estimates of the number still missing could be as high as 50,000. The BBC's Latin America correspondent Will Grant visited towns in La Guaira after the tremors first hit, and returned to find families continuing their search for loved ones a month on.
